Seems like the problem is more articulated than that. In my case (Godot 4.6, Windows 11), the counter works as intended, only that the actual line it jumps to is not always right. I'll try and deep dive into the code to see what the problem is.
EDIT: so i'm actually stupid because the problem i reproduced is the same exact you have, so the problem is the same.
I'm gonna try and see what's the matter with it.

It looks like the issue (or part of it) is in String rfind itself, which doesn't work correctly when setting `p_from`. 
The behavior was changed in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/104332 , cc @Ivorforce @ColinSORourke
Example `"a test 1".rfind("test", 7)` should work, but it returns -1.
I think the check `p_from > len - str_len` that is used in the forward find function doesn't make sense for rfind, since it is an end bound here.

There are other issues too like having the from in the search word working when it shouldn't, like `"a test 1".rfind("test", 3)`.
And there is a string test `MULTICHECK_STRING_INT_EQ(s, rfindn, "WHA", 1000, -1);` that should probably work, reverse searching from 1000 to 0 should find the text.

> It looks like the issue (or part of it) is in String rfind itself, which doesn't work correctly when setting `p_from`. The behavior was changed in [#104332](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/104332)

Indeed, it was modified to be consistent across similar functions.
However, looking at your examples, I think there may a be misunderstanding in how the indices work. Note that #104332 didn't change this aspect — what it changed was that the functions previously sometimes silently ignored indexing errors, and inconsistently handled negative indices. Both have been made consistent by #104332.

> Example `"a test 1".rfind("test", 7)` should work, but it returns -1. 

I disagree, `-1` is the correct return value. If you enter `7` as the starting index, it starts well beyond "test", so it cannot find it:

```
a test 1
01234578
      ^
      test  (no match)
       test (no match)
       (done)
```

> I think the check `p_from > len - str_len` that is used in the forward find function doesn't make sense for rfind, since it is an end bound here.

Nope, the indices are in relation to the start in both `find` and `rfind`. This was the case both before and after #104332. Only negative indices (like `-1`) are in relation to the end of the string to search, both in the case of `find` and `rfind`.

If #104332 affected the outcome, it's probably because `rfind` previously ignored indexing errors and silently started from index `-1`, which also would have been incorrect with an input of `7`.

`rfind` treats `p_from` as the end bound of the search. It is sometimes called start because the search starts there and goes to the start of the string.
Your example treats it as `find`, not `rfind` too, it needs to go backwards.

This is how `rfind_sequence` currently works, going from `p_from` to 0:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/5ad8b27d8db0776700c2b08bf68fbea5e0a4680d/core/templates/span.h#L172-L178

And this behavior was the same beforehand, going to index 0, so the PR indeed didn't change that, but you have it backwards. 

The documentation also says it goes from `from` to the beginning of the string https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_string.html#class-string-method-rfind (though the last added note doesn't really make sense here).

(i had an earlier comment not exactly addressing your point)

I see what you mean now. Indeed, the example would actually look like this:

```
a test 1
01234578
      ^
      test
      (out of bounds; abort)
```

So, when an index beyond the search string is supplied, the `rfind` function simply gives up.
I can see how it could be argued differently: You could jump back to the latest valid position:

```
a test 1
01234578
      ^
      test
      (out of bounds; jump back)
    test
   test
  test
  (match; return 2)
```

However, I think I would find this surprising, since the same wouldn't be possible with `0` going backwards:

```
"a test 1".rfind("test", 0)  // Start at 0
"a test 1".rfind("test", -1)  // Jump to start at 0? Nope, starts at the end instead due to negative indexing behavior.
```

Ok, I see the intent behind it now.

I'm going to use the terms needle and haystack, since "search string" is somewhat ambiguous.

At first I was expecting `p_from` to mark the end of the needle string, not the start of it, like python.
And after I realized it is the start of the needle string, I wasn't concerned with the exact boundaries of where it is possible to find the needle.

> However, I think I would find this surprising, since the same wouldn't be possible with `0` going backwards:

I can see how one might expect this, but since rfind is directional it doesn't need to be symmetric. I wouldn't expect `-1` (ignoring the actual negative index behavior) to work since it is already past `0`. Jumping backwards in the search to just check `0` is different than jumping forward in the search to the first possible position (the last valid index) and starting the search from there.
Also `7` is in bounds of the haystack string itself, so even if the needle **can not** be found there, I would expect it to work as if it just **wasn't** found there and continue searching. 
Though I would probably also expect any value positively out of bounds to do the same.


Where this relates to this issue is in `TextEdit::search`.
It doesn't allow `-1`, and TextEdit doesn't tend to use negative indexes like that.
So currently to search an entire line in reverse you need to use the length of the haystack string minus the length of the needle string as the column parameter, instead of just the last column (haystack length) like before. 
This could be fixed in `TextEdit::search` itself, but I would rather see it in `rfind` as well.

> Ok, I see the intent behind it now.
> 
> I'm going to use the terms needle and haystack, since "search string" is somewhat ambiguous.
> 
> At first I was expecting `p_from` to mark the end of the needle string, not the start of it, like python. 

I'm not sure I understand what you are expecting? `find` and `rfind` indices `from` in Godot behave similar to `find` and `rfind` indices in python.

> And after I realized it is the start of the needle string, I wasn't concerned with the exact boundaries of where it is possible to find the needle.

If you want to enter an index that is relative to the end of the string, you can use negative indices! `-1` starts from the very back, and is therefore the default starting position for `rfind`.

> > However, I think I would find this surprising, since the same wouldn't be possible with `0` going backwards:
> 
> I can see how one might expect this, but since rfind is directional it doesn't need to be symmetric. 

Sure, in `rfind` this wouldn't be useful, but in `find` it might be (as mentioned earlier, the indices are treated the same across both functions).

> Where this relates to this issue is in `TextEdit::search`. It doesn't allow `-1`, and TextEdit doesn't tend to use negative indexes like that. So currently to search an entire line in reverse you need to use the length of the haystack string minus the length of the needle string as the column parameter, instead of just the last column (haystack length) like before. This could be fixed in `TextEdit::search` itself, but I would rather see it in `rfind` as well.

I'm not quite sure how `string.rfind` is used from `TextEdit::search`, but if it's searching from the back, I'd strongly recommend using negative search indices (or just `-1`) because that's the easiest way to index when searching backwards.

If you don't want the usual `String` indexing behavior, you could also use `String.span().rfind(needle, index)` directly. This is the corresponding low-level API, and doesn't do any indexing interpretation (it just uses the index you give it as-is). For example, you could use `haystack.length()` as before, and clamp it to `haystack.length() - needle.length()` yourself (to avoid out-of-bounds indexing).

All that said, I'm not _strongly_ opposed to clamping for out-of-bounds `find` calls. It's not what I would expect it to do, but it should be safe enough, and I can see how it might be the "less surprising" behavior for some people.

In python, `find` and `rfind` both have a `start` and `end` parameter. I meant the `end` parameter since it is closest to how our `rfind` treats `p_from`, but `end` is the last position that the end of the needle can fit, not the last position the start of the needle can be. So pythons `"a test 1".rfind("test", 0, 4)` will not find it, while our `"a test 1".rfind("test", 4)` will. Python effectively only checks index `0` in that example. And passing the length of the haystack as `end` works to search all of it.


`TextEdit::search` uses `-1` when going to the previous line, its just the initial input value that can trigger the out of bounds check here. 
I can clamp it if the direction is backwards, so it works like before.

> In python, `find` and `rfind` both have a `start` and `end` parameter. I meant the `end` parameter since it is closest to how our `rfind` treats `p_from`, but `end` is the last position that the end of the needle can fit, not the last position the start of the needle can be. So pythons `"a test 1".rfind("test", 0, 4)` will not find it, while our `"a test 1".rfind("test", 4)` will. Python effectively only checks index `0` in that example. And passing the length of the haystack as `end` works to search all of it.

I see. I agree that's a good comparison.

> `TextEdit::search` uses `-1` when going to the previous line, its just the initial input value that can trigger the out of bounds check here. I can clamp it if the direction is backwards, so it works like before.

Would this be a good solution for you, or just an awkward workaround? We could bring the potential behavior change into the core meeting, to discuss whether to graciously handle out-of-bounds start indices as the end of the array.
It's fine for this issue, but I might make a proposal for it later.
